doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Joe Williams on race and his marriage
summary: Williams thought prejudice was stupid; his English father-in-law first objected, then bragged about him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What was his view on race relations at that time? Anything that you can remember?

He thought it was pretty stupid. He thought the whole thing was pretty stupid. He was hurt, but I think for example he and his wife had problems. She was a little, white English girl as you know. And there are people who frowned on that. They don’t so much anymore, but at the time — in fact his father-in-law was very upset when he married. Then he found out that the guy that his daughter had married was a famous singer named Joe Williams. Then he became very proud and he bragged to everybody in this little British village that his daughter was married to Joe Williams. And when Joe Williams came to town he was very proud of him. So he thought the initial reaction was dumb. He was proud of black people when they were good. I think he appreciated talent wherever it was. I think he was extremely concerned about people, black people who have a thing about white people, who are prejudiced in that sense. I don’t think he ever would have let race interfere with what was right. I just never found anything to object to in his attitude.
